nodes.name: ʻŌhiʻa lehua
nodes.desc: The most common native tree in Hawaiʻi and often the first to take root on fresh lava. Its nectar feeds honeycreepers, and the fungus behind Rapid ʻŌhiʻa Death threatens it on the Big Island.

nodes.name: Koa
nodes.desc: A native forest tree whose leaves feed caterpillars and other insects, and whose crowns shelter forest birds.

nodes.name: Hāpuʻu tree fern
nodes.desc: A native tree fern of the wet forest understory, growing slowly to a few metres tall.

nodes.name: ʻŌhelo
nodes.desc: A low native shrub of the volcano slopes whose berries are eaten by birds and the nene.

nodes.name: Strawberry guava
nodes.desc: An introduced fruiting tree that invades native forest. Several birds and feral pigs eat its fruit and spread the seeds.

nodes.name: Feral pig
nodes.desc: Introduced omnivore, mostly plant-eating, that roots up the forest floor. The park lists feral pigs among the introduced animals harming its wildlife.

nodes.name: Nēnē
nodes.desc: Hawaiʻi's state bird, a goose that grazes the leaves, seeds, fruit and flowers of grasses and shrubs on lava and shrubland. Introduced mongooses, pigs and cats cut it to 30 birds by 1952.

nodes.name: ʻApapane
nodes.desc: A red honeycreeper that feeds mainly on ʻōhiʻa nectar and also gleans moths and spiders from the canopy. It carries bird malaria, spread by introduced mosquitoes.

nodes.name: ʻIʻiwi
nodes.desc: A scarlet honeycreeper with a long curved bill, recorded in GloBI feeding on ʻōhiʻa flowers.

nodes.name: ʻŌmaʻo
nodes.desc: A native thrush that mainly eats fruit, and also takes insects and small invertebrates.

nodes.name: Moths
nodes.desc: Caterpillars chew native leaves and adult moths are a main food of hoary bats and insect-eating birds.

nodes.name: Black rat
nodes.desc: Introduced omnivore that eats fruit, seeds and eggs. It is prey for hawks, cats and mongooses.

nodes.name: Kalij pheasant
nodes.desc: An introduced game bird, heavily recorded in the park area, that forages on the ground for fruit, seeds and insects. The ʻio takes game birds.

nodes.name: Hawaiʻi ʻelepaio
nodes.desc: A native flycatcher that hunts insects in the forest, and is prey for introduced cats and rats.

nodes.name: Hawaiian hoary bat
nodes.desc: The islands' only native land mammal. It hunts at night, mainly eating moths and beetles, and roosts in trees such as ʻōhiʻa. Federally endangered.

nodes.name: Small Indian mongoose
nodes.desc: Introduced predator, the most recorded mammal in this area. It eats insects, rodents and birds and raids ground nests of birds that evolved without mammal predators.

nodes.name: ʻIo (Hawaiian hawk)
nodes.desc: Endemic hawk that breeds only on the Big Island, in ʻōhiʻa forest. It now eats rats, lizards, game birds and insects, hunting mostly from a perch.

nodes.name: Feral cat
nodes.desc: Introduced top predator with no natural enemy here. It preys on native birds, nesting nene and rodents.

nodes.name: Rain and cloud
nodes.desc: Wet windward slopes feed the rainforest, while the dry Kaʻū side stays arid.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Drives plant growth from the sea-level coast to the high summit.

nodes.name: Lava and volcanic soil
nodes.desc: New flows start as bare rock, and pioneers such as ʻōhiʻa colonise them and slowly build soil.

nodes.name: Fungi and bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead leaves, fern trunks and carcasses, returning nutrients to the soil.
